explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, "you were sold for your iniquities, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away." He names their own sins as the reason. I think that's a hard line to hear, but He says it plainly.

Nope, friend, the verse never mentions any debt of His. The LORD asks which of His creditors He sold them to, and then He answers it Himself. "Look, you were sold for your iniquities." So the reason is their sins, not a bill.

I see why that sounds right, since being sold usually sounds like somebody else's doing. But this verse never mentions enemies. It says, "you were sold for your iniquities, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away." The reason the LORD gives is their own sins.

Careful, friend, those two questions are not a confession. The LORD asks, "Is My hand too short to redeem you?" and the very next thing He does is point to His power. He says, "My rebuke dries up the sea." Nothing in these verses says His strength has run out.

Right, baker. He asks if His hand is too short and if He lacks the strength to deliver, and then He answers with a show of power. "Behold, My rebuke dries up the sea; I turn the rivers into a desert." Nobody says that kind of thing while running low on strength.
Yes, baker. He says, "My rebuke dries up the sea." One rebuke and a whole sea is dry. That's the power He's pointing to.
A split sea is a famous picture, I know. But this verse says something else: "My rebuke dries up the sea." The sea gets dried up, not divided. Read the verse slowly and you'll see it.

That sounds gentle, friend, but this verse isn't gentle. It says, "My rebuke dries up the sea." The sea goes dry, and the rivers turn into a desert right after it. The waves don't get a calm. They get taken away.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, "I clothe the heavens in black and make sackcloth their covering." The sea is dry, the rivers are desert, and now the sky is dressed in black. He keeps going because there's more to say about what He can do.

It's in there, friend. Right after the dried-up sea, the LORD says, "I clothe the heavens in black and make sackcloth their covering." So the statement is true. Go back and look at verse 3, it's the last line of that part.

That's the one, baker. The speaker says, "He awakens Me morning by morning; He awakens My ear to listen as a disciple." Morning after morning, the ear gets woken up to listen. Meanwhile my snooze button wins about every round, and nobody's proud of that.

explanations.answer: Sends Him a dream at night
explanations.explanation: I get it, dreams feel like a natural guess. But the verse talks about mornings, not nights. The speaker says, "He awakens Me morning by morning; He awakens My ear to listen as a disciple." What gets woken up is His ear.

explanations.answer: Shows Him a vision of heaven
explanations.explanation: That would be quite a morning, friend. But this verse never mentions a vision. It says, "He awakens My ear to listen as a disciple." The speaker is waking up to listen.

Yes, baker. The speaker says, "The Lord GOD has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious, nor have I turned back." Ears open, no rebellion, no turning back. All three go together in that one verse.
The verse says the opposite, friend. The speaker says, "I have not been rebellious, nor have I turned back." He says it right after saying the Lord GOD opened His ears. So the statement is true.

I see why you'd think so, since most people would hide. But the speaker says the opposite. "I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle." I think that's a heavy verse, and He stays right there through it.

That's right, baker. The speaker says, "I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle." Verse 6 is a heavy one, with strikes and torn-out beard. I think it's worth noticing that He doesn't hide His face.
Yes, baker. The speaker says, "I have set My face like flint." Flint is a hard stone, so it's a picture of a face that won't budge. He says it because the Lord GOD helps Him.
Water is a fine thing, friend, but you can't set it. It runs wherever it wants. The verse says, "I have set My face like flint," which is a hard stone.
Wax is a good guess if you want something you can shape. But wax gets soft fast, just like chocolate chips in a hot oven. The verse says, "I have set My face like flint," which is a hard stone.
That's it, baker. The speaker says, "The One who vindicates Me is near." Then comes the challenge, "Who will dare to contend with Me?" The nearness comes first, and then the questions.
Close to the sound of it, but the verse never says anything about silence. It says, "The One who vindicates Me is near." Near is the word the speaker uses.
The verse says the opposite, friend. "The One who vindicates Me is near." Near, not far off. That's why the speaker can ask, "Who will dare to contend with Me?"

Yes, baker. The speaker says, "they will all wear out like a garment; the moths will devour them." It's a picture of something wearing out. It comes right after the speaker asks, "Who is there to condemn Me?"

A candle does burn down, so I see the thinking. But this verse never mentions one. It says, "they will all wear out like a garment; the moths will devour them." A garment, and moths are in the picture too.
A field is a solid guess, friend, since the Bible has plenty of them. But not here. The verse says, "they will all wear out like a garment; the moths will devour them." The word is garment.
Right, baker. The verse says, "Let him trust in the name of the LORD; let him lean on his God." The person in the dark with no light is told to trust. That's all the verse tells him to do.
Waiting for morning makes sense to me, friend. But the verse doesn't say it. It says, "Let him trust in the name of the LORD; let him lean on his God." The instruction is to trust.

Nope, that's not in the verse. The one walking in darkness is told, "Let him trust in the name of the LORD; let him lean on his God." Trust and lean, those are the two things. Verse 11 is where people light their own fires.

That's what the verse says, baker. "You will lie down in a place of torment." This one is heavy, and I won't joke about it. It's spoken to those who kindle fires and walk in the light of their own fire.

Rest would be a nice thing to hear, friend, but that's not what the verse says. The words are, "You will lie down in a place of torment." It's a heavy verse. It speaks to those who walk in the light of fires they lit.

I understand why it might sound that way, since the people had lit their own fires and arrayed themselves with firebrands. But the verse says, "You will lie down in a place of torment." It's heavy, so I'll just say it plainly.
